title: Pattern kinds (declaration, property, relational, list, and logical patterns)
hook: A ragged comma-separated values (CSV) import row is a list pattern problem. A Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) launch payload is a property pattern problem. Name the kind, then write the arm.

blocks.text: Patterns are mini-tests you attach to is expressions and switch arms. C# provides many kinds: declaration and type patterns check runtime type and optionally bind a variable; constant patterns match a value including null; relational patterns compare to constants; property and positional patterns match object shape; list patterns match sequence position; logical and, or, and not combine other patterns. The discard _ matches anything left.

entries.plainDefinition: Tests whether a value is of a type and, if so, assigns it to a new variable in scope.
entries.example: if (seq is IList<string> list) uses the list variable only when the cast succeeds.

entries.plainDefinition: Matches one or more properties by name and nested pattern, like { Scheme: "LTI", Version: "1.3" }.
entries.example: Matches a record without calling Deconstruct — property names must match.

entries.plainDefinition: Matches elements at positions in an array or list-like sequence, with .. slice for "any number of elements here."
entries.example: [_, "DEPOSIT", .., var amount] skips middle columns and binds the last cell.

entries.plainDefinition: Compares the input to a constant using <, >, <=, or >= inside a pattern context.
entries.example: < 50 => "fail" in a switch expression on an int.

blocks.text: Choosing the right pattern kind keeps branching declarative. Relational patterns express score bands without nested ifs. Property patterns describe auth token records by shape. List patterns handle CSV rows whose column count varies. Logical patterns combine conditions with and, or, not — not with && inside the pattern itself. The compiler checks reachability so you do not accidentally shadow a specific arm with a catch-all var.

blocks.title: is not null
blocks.body: Prefer value is not null over value != null when you care about pattern matching semantics. is not null is a logical not pattern and ignores overloaded == operators.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Need a type check plus variable?
items.body: Use a declaration pattern: input is SomeType name.

items.title: Need to match fields on a record?
items.body: Use a property pattern: { Field: pattern, Other: { } }.

items.title: Need numeric or ordered ranges?
items.body: Use relational patterns, combined with and / or / not: (> 32) and (< 212).

items.title: Need position in a sequence?
items.body: Use list patterns with .. to skip a variable middle: [first, _, .., last].

diagram.title: Pattern kind decision tree

snippet.label: Relational bands on an attempt score
snippet.explanation: Each < arm is a relational pattern. Order matters: after < 50, only 50–99 reach < 70. The or arm rejects impossible percents before bands run.

snippet.label: List pattern on a CSV row
snippet.explanation: WITHDRAWAL rows have a variable number of middle columns. .. skips them. var amount binds the last cell. DEPOSIT assumes a fixed layout with amount in the fourth column.

snippet.label: Property pattern and is not null
snippet.explanation: Property patterns match Scheme and bind ExpiresAt. not null is a logical not on the constant null pattern. The boolean && after is is ordinary C# — guards that need arbitrary logic go outside the pattern.

blocks.text: JavaScript destructuring — const [_, kind, ...rest] = row — pulls values at run time and may yield undefined. C# list patterns are compile-checked matches that fail to the next switch arm when the shape does not fit. TypeScript discriminated unions narrow on a tag field; C# property patterns can match several fields at once without a single required discriminator, though records with a Kind property are the clearest design.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Writing && inside a pattern instead of and. Matching [a, b] on an IEnumerable that is not a countable list — list patterns need an indexer sequence. Putting a var catch-all arm before specific arms, making later arms unreachable. Using constant "1.3" when the wire sends "1.3.0" — normalize or add a when guard.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: property patterns on records are how you implement discriminated unions without a single Kind field — match Scheme and Version together. List patterns on CSV import rows catch ragged shapes at parse time instead of IndexOutOfRangeException later. Roslyn CS8510 flags unreachable arms when a var or _ catch-all sits before specific property patterns — run dotnet build with warnings as errors in CI.

snippet.label: Property patterns as discriminated union without explicit tag
snippet.explanation: Line 5: property patterns match multiple fields like TS union without kind if Scheme is reliable. Line 12: list pattern with .. slice validates CSV shape before allocation.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Needs indexer sequence, not bare IEnumerable
Later arms unreachable if order wrong

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Using && inside a pattern instead of and. Matching list patterns on IEnumerable without an indexer. Putting var catch-all before specific property patterns. Confusing TypeScript destructuring (runtime, may be undefined) with C# list patterns (compile-checked, fails to next arm).

interviewTakeaways: Pattern kinds — declaration, property, relational, list, logical — compose in switch arms; order is semantic.
Property patterns implement discriminated-union-style narrowing on records without a single tag field.
List patterns with .. guard CSV ragged rows; require countable indexer sequences.
60s: Property patterns = multi-field union narrow. List + .. for import shapes. and/or/not not &&. var catch-all last or CS8510 unreachable arm.
Follow-up: when is a positional pattern preferable to property patterns on a record?
commonPitfalls: Writing && inside a pattern instead of and gets you rejected — use and, or, not combinators.
Matching [a, b] on IEnumerable without indexer — list patterns need IList or array.
Strong answer: 'Property patterns for auth records. List patterns for CSV. Relational for score bands. Catch-all last. Discard throws on unknown.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: const [_, kind, ...rest] = row is runtime destructuring. C# list patterns are compile-checked matches that can fail to the next arm. JavaScript destructuring throws or yields undefined.

TS narrows on token.kind === 'lti'. C# property patterns match { Scheme: 'LTI', Issuer: not null } in one arm — multiple fields at once without a single required discriminator, though explicit tags are clearer.
